newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Lack of approvals hamper Malaysia's short-selling.
newsitem.headline: Lack of approvals hamper Malaysia's short-selling.

text.p: One week after its launch, regulated short-selling of stocks in Malaysia has attracted no volume, hampered by a lack of approvals for participants and slow infrastructure set-ups, dealers said.
As of late Friday, no transactions had been recorded, market regulators said.
Short-selling is where an investor sells securities he does not own, hoping to replace them with the same stocks at a lower price. The investor profits from the difference in price.
Until Sept 30, short-selling was illegal, and investors in the past have been charged for failing to deliver scrip for the entire amount of stocks sold short.
Short-selling is used for arbitrage on stocks as well as to hedge portfolios.

But under Malaysia's approved guidelines, participants must make arrangements with approved Securities Borrowing and Lending (SBL) agents in order to avoid the occurrence of "naked", or uncovered, short-selling.
Malaysian regulators last week released a list of 50 stocks -- mostly highly liquid, well-capitalised blue chips -- that can be sold short.
"Only one stockbroking company was approved (as an SBL agent)," said William Chan, an institutional dealer with Seagroatt & Campbell. "It will be months before you see any activity," he predicted.

Rashid Hussain Securities is so far the only brokerage approved as an SBL agent. A Securities Commission spokeswoman said that "four to five" other applications are also being considered. "We're expecting more (to apply)," she added.
Another impediment to the short-selling start-up is the lack of infrastructure at brokerage firms, such as software by which firms keep track of transactions.

"We are allowed to short-sell, but we don't have approval from the SC (Securities Commission), we don't have the software. Most brokers have the same problem," said a dealer at a local bank-linked brokerage firm.
An analyst at another domestic firm said approval as an SBL agent for her firm was still pending. "People aren't ready to do short-selling," she said.

Analysts said even after the basic arrangements are in place, investors and market participants will have to be educated about the practice, which will pave the way for Malaysia to begin trading of stock options and stock index options.
Presently, only stock futures are traded on the benchmark Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index.
"It will take some time before people get used to it," one institutional dealer said.
